{{short description|British physicist and computer scientist}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Jenifer Leech''' (née '''Wheildon Brown'''; later '''Haselgrove'''; 3 August 1930 – 13 March 2015<!--Dates confirmed by family via OTRS, see talk page-->) was a British physicist and computer scientist. She is most noted for her formulation of [[Ray tracing (physics)|ray tracing]] equations in a cold magneto-[[plasma (physics)|plasma]], now widely known in the [[radio]] science community<ref>{{cite web |editor-last=Lagasse |editor-first=Paul |date=June 2008 |pages=14–55 |url=https://www.ursi.org/files/RSBissues/RSB_325_2008_06.pdf |title=Special Sections Honoring Jenifer Haselgrove |work=Radio Science Bulletin |issn=1024-4530 |accessdate=16 July 2011  |quote=Please enjoy this tribute to Jenifer Haselgrove and her achievements. In collating and researching for this work, we have been inspired by many of the great minds that have brought us so far in radio science, but none more than Jenifer Haselgrove and those around her at Cambridge, which led to her famous formulation and her use of one of mankind's first computers to solve it.<sup>[p. 16]</sup>}}</ref> as Haselgrove's Equations.<ref>K. G. Budden : "The Propagation of Radio Waves: The Theory of Radio Waves of Low Power in the Ionosphere and Magnetosphere" Cambridge University Press, 1988.</ref><ref name="kelso1964">J. M. Kelso : "Radio ray propagation in the ionosphere", McGraw-Hill, 1964, 408 pp. [https://books.google.com/books?id=qSQ5AAAAIAAJ] [http://lccn.loc.gov/63015022]</ref>

==Haselgrove's equations==
Haselgrove developed her equations at [[Cambridge University]] in the 1950s, as a student under [[Kenneth Budden]], by re-applying the earlier work of [[William Rowan Hamilton]]  and [[Hamilton's principle]] in [[geometrical optics]]<ref>A. W. Conway and J. L. Synge, The Mathematical Papers of  Sir William Rowan Hamilton Vol 1. Gemoetrical Optics, London, Cambridge University Press, 1931.</ref> to [[radio propagation]] in a plasma.<ref>Haselgrove, J.: 1955, Ray Theory and a New Method for Ray Tracing, London Physical Society Report of Conference on the Physics of the Ionosphere. pp. 355–364.</ref> Indeed, the application of Haselgrove's equations is often termed Hamiltonian ray tracing. Ray tracing is intrinsically an approximation that is often called geometric. It formulates as the [[Eikonal equation]] and is only applicable under certain conditions including that the plasma is slowly varying; nevertheless it has enormous practical use in radio science.  Other radio propagation scientists have developed various techniques to explore radio propagation in such media,<ref name=kelso1964/>  but Haselgrove's formulation has seen the most widespread application, most likely because the resulting set of differential equations readily lend themselves to numerical solution on a computer. Haselgrove herself used the Cambridge computer, [[EDSAC]], to study ray propagation in the Earth's ionosphere in the late 1950s.<ref>{{cite web |editor-last=Hartley |editor-first=David |year=1999 |url=https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/conference/EDSAC99/reminiscences/ |title=EDSAC 1 and after&nbsp;– a compilation of personal reminiscences |work=EDSAC 99 |accessdate=16 July 2011}}</ref> Historically the best-known code applying Haselgrove's equations is  the Jones-Stephenson code<ref>Jones, R. M. and Stephenson, J. J. A versatile three-dimensional ray tracing computer program for radio waves in the ionosphere, U. S. Department of Commerce, OT Report 75-76, 1975.</ref> which was developed in the 1970s and may be found at the US Department of Commerce website.

Today Haselgrove's equations are widely used in scientific investigations involving radio propagation in slowly varying plasmas, and therefore have found much applicability in exploration and utilization of the Earth's [[ionosphere]]. Here they have also been used to represent the radio propagation element of practical systems providing [[high frequency]] communication, [[direction finding]] and [[over-the-horizon radar]]. For a recent broad discussion on ray tracing in the ionosphere see Bennett ''et al''.<ref>J. A. Bennett, P. L. Dyson, R. J. Norman, Progress in Radio Ray Tracing in the Ionosphere, ''The Radio Science Bulletin'', September 2004, p. 81.</ref> Other publications applying Haselgrove's equations have recently appeared.<ref>C. J. Coleman, On the simulation of backscatter ionograms, J.A.T.P. 59, 16, pg 20-89, 1997.<br />• R. I. Barnes, Faraday Rotation in a cold, inhomogeneous magneto-plasma: A numerical comparison of ray and full wave analyses, Rad. Sci. 32, 1523-1532, 1997.<br />• X. Huang and B. Reinisch, Real-time HF ray tracing through a tilted ionosphere,  Radio Science, 41,5, 2006<br />• L. J. Nickisch, M. A. Hausman and S. V. Fridman, Range rate-Doppler correlation for HF propagation in TID environments, Radio Science 41, 2006.</ref>

==Personal life==
Haselgrove was married to British mathematician [[C. Brian Haselgrove]] and published several highly cited, technical articles with him, example; C. B. Haselgrove and Jenifer Haselgrove,  Twisted Ray Paths in the Ionosphere, Proc. Phys. Soc. 75 No 3 (1 March 1960) 357–363. They are also credited for first solving the 6×10 [[Pentomino]]. Brian Haselgrove died in 1964, and Jenifer remarried to another British mathematician, [[John Leech (mathematician)|John Leech]], and took his surname. She worked at the [[University of Glasgow]] until 1982. She resided in England until her death on 13 March 2015.
